title: Who Can Install Bathroom Tile and Fixtures in a Collingwood Home?
seoTitle: Who Can Install Bathroom Tile and Fixtures in a Collingwood…
seoDescription: Find out who can install bathroom tile, vanities, toilets, faucets, plumbing, waterproofing, and electrical fixtures in a Collingwood, Ontario home, with…
html:
Key takeaways

  • A handyman, tile installer, or renovation contractor can handle tile and finish work in a Collingwood, Ontario bathroom.
  • New, relocated, or altered plumbing belongs with the appropriate Ontario plumbing trade because plumbing is a compulsory trade.
  • A limited like-for-like fixture replacement is different from work that changes piping, drains, walls, floors, structure, or fixture locations.
  • Collingwood’s posted building-permit review timelines for complete applications range from 10 to 30 business days depending on building class.
  • Only a Licensed Electrical Contractor can be hired to perform electrical work in an Ontario home, subject to limited legal exemptions.
  • A single renovation contractor can coordinate the project, but the written scope should identify the plumbing and electrical contractors, permits, inspections, waterproofing system, and warranty responsibilities.

In Collingwood, Ontario, a handyman, tile installer, or renovation contractor can handle bathroom tile and finish work, while licensed plumbing and electrical contractors handle new or altered plumbing and electrical systems.

That division applies to homes, rental properties, and many cottages in the Collingwood area. Rural properties may involve additional access, water-supply, septic, or seasonal-use considerations, so confirm that the contractor serves the specific property before signing a contract.

Who can install bathroom tile in a Collingwood home?

A handyman, tile installer, or bathroom renovation contractor can install bathroom tile, provided the contractor has the skills and equipment required for the specified work.

Typical tile-setting tasks include:

  • Removing existing tile and disposing of debris
  • Inspecting and preparing floors, walls, and other substrates
  • Installing approved backer board or other tile underlayment
  • Measuring and laying out tile patterns
  • Cutting and setting ceramic, porcelain, stone, or mosaic tile
  • Grouting and sealing tile surfaces
  • Replacing cracked or damaged tiles
  • Finishing edges around vanities, tubs, toilets, and other fixtures

Ontario classifies Terrazzo, Tile and Marble Setter as a non-compulsory trade, so a provincial Certificate of Qualification is not required solely to perform tile-setting work. That classification does not prove that every installer is competent, and it does not remove building-code, waterproofing, permit, manufacturer, or contractual requirements.

What to confirm before hiring a tile installer

Request a written scope that identifies:

  • The substrate being tiled and the repairs included
  • The underlayment or backer-board system
  • The wet-area waterproofing system
  • Tile, grout, sealant, and trim products
  • Drainage slopes and transitions where applicable
  • Protection of adjacent walls, floors, and fixtures
  • Tile removal, disposal, cleanup, and warranty responsibility

Surface preparation and coordination are different from installing a complete shower waterproofing system. Shower waterproofing should follow the selected system manufacturer’s requirements and applicable building standards, including compatible membranes, seams, corners, penetrations, slopes, and drainage details.

Who can install a bathroom vanity, toilet, faucet, or shower fixture?

A handyman or renovation contractor can install cabinets, countertops, trim, mirrors, hardware, and other finish components, while a licensed plumbing trade should perform new, relocated, or altered plumbing work.

Task-by-task scope

Bathroom taskTypical responsible contractorWhat the written scope should state
Install a vanity cabinet in the existing locationHandyman, cabinet installer, or renovation contractorCabinet assembly, anchoring, countertop, filler panels, trim, and caulking
Install a vanity countertop or backsplashCountertop, tile, or renovation contractorMeasurements, cutouts, support, sealant, backsplash, and finish details
Mount a mirror or bathroom accessoriesHandyman or renovation contractorAnchoring method, wall protection, and whether electrical connections are excluded
Replace tile or groutHandyman, tile installer, or renovation contractorRemoval, substrate repair, tile setting, grout, sealant, and cleanup
Replace a toilet in the same locationPlumbing-qualified installer or plumberShutoff, flange condition, supply connection, waste connection, leak testing, and disposal
Replace a faucet using existing connectionsPlumbing-qualified installer or plumberShutoff valves, supply lines, drain connection, leak testing, and any required repairs
Replace a sink using the existing opening and connectionsPlumbing-qualified installer or plumberCountertop or vanity fit, drain and supply connections, leak testing, and sealant
Replace shower trim using existing compatible plumbingPlumbing-qualified installer or plumberCompatibility, cartridge or valve condition, escutcheon sealing, and leak testing
Install new supply piping or drain pipingLicensed plumbing tradePlumbing design, materials, access, testing, permits, and inspections
Move a toilet, sink, tub, or showerLicensed plumbing trade and renovation contractorNew layout, drain and vent changes, supply piping, wall or floor opening, permits, and restoration

A limited like-for-like replacement means removing an existing fixture and installing a compatible replacement without changing walls, structural elements, supply piping, drains, vents, electrical wiring, or the fixture location. That narrow scenario may not require a building permit, but the permit treatment must be confirmed with the Town of Collingwood for the actual scope.

Replacing a fixture is not automatically permit-free when the work changes plumbing connections, piping, drains, walls, floors, structural elements, or the surrounding construction.

What plumbing work requires a licensed trade?

Plumbing is a compulsory trade in Ontario. Legally performing the trade requires the appropriate Ontario registration or certificate status, and the person’s information must appear on the Skilled Trades Ontario Public Register.

Assign the following work to the licensed plumbing trade responsible for the project:

  • Installing new water-supply piping
  • Relocating a toilet, sink, tub, or shower
  • Altering drains, waste piping, or vents
  • Installing or changing a shower valve or rough-in
  • Roughing in a new bathroom or washroom
  • Connecting plumbing where the existing arrangement is not suitable
  • Repairing concealed leaks or damaged plumbing behind finished surfaces
  • Completing plumbing tests and required inspections

A renovation contractor may coordinate this work, but the quote should identify the plumbing contractor by name, define the plumbing scope, and state who obtains permits and schedules inspections.

When does a Collingwood bathroom project need a building permit?

A Collingwood bathroom project requires permit review when its scope includes construction, bathroom rough-ins, new plumbing piping, relocated plumbing, or other work regulated by the Ontario Building Code.

Permit treatment depends on the complete project scope rather than the fixture name alone. A project can move from cosmetic work into permit-required construction when it opens walls or floors, changes plumbing, affects structure, alters ventilation, or creates a new bathroom or washroom.

Examples that commonly require permit review include:

  • Roughing in a new bathroom or washroom
  • Installing new plumbing piping
  • Relocating a toilet, sink, tub, or shower
  • Changing drain, waste, or vent piping
  • Altering construction behind a shower or wet area
  • Removing or changing structural walls or floor systems
  • Creating a new bathroom in an unfinished space

The Town’s current posted building-permit review timelines for complete applications are:

  • 10 business days: single residential dwelling
  • 15 business days: Part 9 buildings, including multi-family residential and certain commercial or industrial buildings under 600 square metres and not over three storeys
  • 20 business days: Part 3 residential, commercial, or industrial buildings over 600 square metres or more than three storeys
  • 30 business days: post-disaster buildings

These are building-permit review timelines by building class, not guaranteed completion dates for a bathroom renovation. Incomplete drawings, missing information, zoning review, revisions, inspections, plumbing-permit requirements, and other approvals can extend the overall schedule.

Permit decision matrix

Project scopePermit approach
Replace damaged tile without changing plumbing, structure, or electrical systemsUsually a finish-work project; confirm if demolition exposes regulated construction
Paint, caulk, install trim, mount a mirror, or install accessoriesUsually finish work when no wiring, structural work, or regulated alteration is involved
Replace a compatible toilet, faucet, or sink in the same locationLimited like-for-like work may not require a building permit; confirm the actual scope with Collingwood
Replace a vanity while keeping the plumbing layout unchangedCabinet and finish work may be handled by a renovation contractor; plumbing connections still require proper installation
Install new supply piping or relocate drainsPermit review and licensed plumbing work are required
Rough in a new bathroom or washroomPermit review, plumbing coordination, inspections, and code-compliant construction are required
Add or relocate wiring, receptacles, lights, fans, or heated flooringElectrical notification and electrical-safety requirements apply; use a Licensed Electrical Contractor

Who can do electrical work in a bathroom renovation?

Only a Licensed Electrical Contractor can be hired to perform electrical work in an Ontario home, subject to limited legal exemptions.

Electrical work includes:

  • Installing or relocating bathroom lights
  • Wiring an illuminated mirror
  • Installing or wiring an exhaust fan
  • Adding or relocating receptacles or switches
  • Installing electric heated flooring
  • Running new cable behind walls or ceilings
  • Connecting new electrical equipment

Non-electrical work does not automatically require an electrical contractor. Mounting a mirror, installing a vanity, replacing a decorative fixture without changing wiring, or attaching accessories can remain finish work when no electrical connection or wiring alteration is involved.

Ask for the contractor’s seven-digit ECRA/ESA licence number when electrical work is included, and request the ESA Certificate of Acceptance after the work is complete. A general contractor or handyman can coordinate electrical work, but the electrical portion must be completed through the properly licensed electrical contracting business.

Can one contractor coordinate tile, fixtures, plumbing, and electrical work?

Yes, one renovation contractor can coordinate the project while licensed plumbing and electrical contractors complete the regulated portions.

A practical sequence is:

1. Confirm the layout and choose the tile, vanity, fixtures, fan, lighting, and accessories.

2. Separate finish work from plumbing, electrical, structural, and permit-related work.

3. Confirm whether the project requires a building permit, plumbing permit, ESA notification, or inspection.

4. Complete demolition and inspect exposed walls, floors, drains, wiring, and substrates.

5. Perform plumbing and electrical rough-ins.

6. Complete required inspections before closing walls or floors.

7. Install the shower waterproofing system according to its manufacturer’s instructions.

8. Install backer board, tile, grout, sealant, vanity, trim, mirrors, and accessories.

9. Install final plumbing and electrical fixtures.

10. Test for leaks, verify drainage and ventilation, complete ESA documentation, and correct deficiencies.

When comparing contractors, treat coordination as a service responsibility rather than proof that the contractor personally performs every trade. The contract should identify who performs each task and who is accountable for permits, inspections, warranty claims, and repairs.

Red flags in a bathroom renovation quote

A quote needs clarification when it:

  • Says “bathroom renovation” without listing individual tasks
  • Uses “fixture installation” without identifying whether plumbing connections are included
  • Promises waterproofing without naming the membrane or system
  • Describes plumbing as “minor” without identifying piping, drains, vents, or valves
  • Includes electrical work but does not name the Licensed Electrical Contractor
  • Assigns permit responsibility to “the homeowner” without listing the permits required
  • Excludes substrate repairs even though tile removal is included
  • Provides no leak-testing, inspection, cleanup, or warranty terms
  • Uses a low lump-sum price that excludes disposal, fixture modifications, access repairs, or concealed-condition work

What should a homeowner request before work starts?

Request these documents and details before approving the project:

  • A room-by-room written scope
  • A task-by-task division between finish work, plumbing, and electrical work
  • Names and licence details for the plumbing and electrical contractors
  • Permit and inspection responsibility in writing
  • The shower waterproofing product and installation method
  • Product specifications for tile, grout, sealant, fixtures, fans, and heated flooring
  • A demolition and disposal plan
  • A change-order process for concealed damage
  • Payment milestones and warranty terms
  • Proof of insurance from the businesses actually performing the work
  • Final inspection records, ESA documentation, and product manuals where applicable

FAQ

Can a handyman install bathroom tile in Collingwood?

Yes. A handyman can install bathroom tile, grout, sealant, trim, and related finishes when the person has demonstrated tile experience and the project does not include regulated plumbing, electrical, structural, or permit-required work.

Can a handyman replace a toilet or faucet?

A handyman may handle a limited like-for-like replacement when the existing location, piping, drains, and connections remain unchanged, but the actual plumbing scope determines who should perform the work and whether permit review applies.

Does replacing a bathroom vanity require a permit?

Replacing a vanity as cabinet and finish work generally does not create a building-permit requirement by itself, but changes to plumbing, walls, floors, structure, wiring, or the fixture location can change the permit analysis.

Who should waterproof a shower before tile is installed?

The contractor installing the shower waterproofing system should follow the system manufacturer’s requirements for substrate preparation, seams, corners, penetrations, slopes, and drainage, and the written scope should identify the specific waterproofing system rather than describing the work only as “waterproofing preparation.”

Does every bathroom fixture replacement require an electrician?

No. Mounting a mirror, installing a vanity, replacing trim, or completing other non-electrical finish work does not automatically require an electrician, while new or altered wiring, receptacles, lighting, fans, illuminated mirrors, and heated floors require a Licensed Electrical Contractor.

Can one contractor manage the entire bathroom renovation?

Yes. One renovation contractor can manage scheduling, finishes, and subcontractor coordination while licensed plumbing and electrical contractors perform the regulated portions and the contract clearly assigns responsibility for permits, inspections, testing, and warranties.
